content: Pulmonary edema, cerebral malaria, pancytopenia, jaundice, splenic rupture, hemoglobinuria, acute renal failure, and shock are potential complications of severe malaria. Immediate and effective treatment should follow the same protocols as for severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria. After initial treatment with parenteral artesunate, therapy can be completed with a full course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) or chloroquine in regions where chloroquine remains the preferred treatment. Radical cure with primaquine should be administered after recovery. Artesunate is supplied as a powder of artesunic acid, which is dissolved in 5% sodium bicarbonate to form sodium artesunate. This solution is then diluted in approximately 5 mL of 5% dextrose and administered either intravenously or intramuscularly into the anterior thigh. The solution must be freshly prepared for each administration and should not be stored. Artesunate is rapidly hydrolyzed in vivo to dihydroartemisinin, the primary antimalarial agent. Pharmacokinetic studies in children with severe malaria indicate that younger children have lower exposure to both artesunate and its active metabolite, dihydroartemisinin, compared to older children and adults. Body weight has been identified as a significant factor in pharmacokinetics, suggesting that younger children have a larger apparent volume of distribution and may require slightly higher doses of parenteral artesunate to achieve comparable drug exposure. Delayed hemolysis, occurring more than one week after artesunate treatment for severe malaria, has been reported in hyperparasitemic, non-immune travelers. Between 2010 and 2012, six reports documented delayed hemolysis in 19 European travelers treated with artesunate injections. Most of these cases involved adults, with a median age of 50 years (range: 5–71 years). A similar phenomenon was observed in 7% of hyperparasitemic African children in a prospective study. Artesunate rapidly kills ring-stage parasites, which are then removed from red blood cells by the spleen. These infected erythrocytes are returned to circulation with a shortened lifespan, leading to the observed hemolysis. This post-treatment hemolysis is a predictable consequence of artesunate’s life-saving effects. Hyperparasitemic patients should be closely monitored for late-onset anemia. The dosing subgroup reviewed pharmacokinetic data from 71 adults and 265 children treated with artesunate for severe malaria. Simulations showed underexposure in younger children. Revised parenteral dosing regimens are predicted to provide equivalent artesunate and dihydroartemisinin exposures across all age groups. Doses of 4 mg/kg have been studied without observed toxicity. The benefits of improved antimalarial exposure in children outweigh any potential risks. Artemether, a less active compound than its metabolite dihydroartemisinin, can be administered intramuscularly or orally. In severe falciparum malaria, intramuscular artemether is absorbed more slowly and erratically compared to water-soluble artesunate, which is absorbed rapidly and reliably. These pharmacological differences likely explain the clinical superiority of parenteral artesunate over artemether in severe malaria. Artemether is dispensed in an oil-based solution and administered intramuscularly into the anterior thigh. Quinine, historically used for severe malaria, is available in various salts, with the dihydrochloride form being the most common for parenteral use. Intramuscular and intravenous administration achieve similar peak concentrations. A loading dose of 20 mg salt/kg body weight provides therapeutic plasma concentrations within 4 hours, followed by maintenance doses of 10 mg salt/kg every 8 hours. Rapid intravenous administration of quinine is dangerous and must be given as a slow, rate-controlled infusion over 4 hours. Intramuscular injections should be administered to the anterior thigh to avoid sciatic nerve injury. Undiluted quinine dihydrochloride is acidic and painful; buffered formulations or diluted solutions are preferred. Gluconate salts are less acidic and better tolerated. Parenteral artesunate is recommended as the first-line treatment for severe malaria in adults, children, infants, and pregnant women in all trimesters. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is preferred over quinine. Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that parenteral artesunate prevents more deaths than quinine in both adults and children. Although artemether and quinine are comparable in children, artemether may be superior in older children and adults.
